Recently I was sorely disappointed by the novel “The Hummingbird” which tells the story of a married man who has never been able to be with the true love of his life. I was reminded how much the structure of a novel can really impact how successfully it conveys its subject when reading Miranda Cowley Heller's emotionally-intelligent debut novel “The Paper Palace” because the central story is the same as Veroensi's but much more effective. Elle Bishop is a happily married wife and mother staying at her family's summer camp in Cape Cod. On the evening before the book's opening chapter, she finally had sex with Jonas, a man she's been in love with since she was a teenager but who she's not been able to be with for complicated reasons. We follow the fallout of this over a 24 hour period while getting the story of her difficult family life and events leading up to this disarming experience. We also come to understand the dark secret which simultaneously binds her to Jonas and keeps them physically apart. Wish You Were Here by Jodi Picoult was a very moving and timely novel. I had read some advanced reviews about what this book was about but they were not able to prepare me for how reading Wish You Were Here was going to affect me. Jodi Picoult was able to capture all the underlying fears, warnings, precautions, attitudes, compliance and non-compliance to the threat of Covid-19 as it overtook and cast its ugly face upon the world. Her extensive research was masterful. She captured the essence of the bewilderment, terror, stress, pure exhaustion and the determination to not let the virus win that the members of the health care community faced. The challenges of living in quarantine, excessive hand washing, securing time slots for food delivery, the process of wiping down and washing everything that would be touched, gathering mail and delaying its opening, mask wearing, overcrowded hospitals and the exorbitant amount of patients put on ventilators only to die were all present throughout. All those things and more was what made this book so believable. Jodi Picoult captured those moments of crisis so many of us faced and also the resilience that so many exhibited to be able to navigate their way through the pandemic. Wish You Were Here was well written and so memorable. Diana O’Toole was an almost thirty year old woman that was living her life according to her plan. She was an associate specialist at the well known and renowned Sotherby’s. Diana had high aspirations to climb the corporate ladder in the art field at Sotherby’s and secure a prominent position. Her private life was equally satisfying. Her long term boyfriend, Finn, was a surgical resident at a prominent New York hospital. Their futures were promising and together they contemplated an engagement and eventually marriage and a home in nearby Westchester County. Diana and Finn had saved for and meticulously planned a vacation to the Galapoaos Islands that would occur just before Diana’s thirty birthday. Diana even suspected that Finn would finally propose to her there and of course she would say yes. Just at that time, Covid-19 had made its way to New York City. Diana noticed how empty the streets were and how few people were out and about. As Diana traveled around the city by subway, the day before her and Finn’s vacation, she noticed how deserted the subway stations and cars were. When Diana got home, she was not prepared for what Finn was about to tell her. Finn’s role at the hospital had been redefined. All doctors, residents and medical staff were required to be available to treat the onslaught of patients that arrived at the hospital with symptoms of COVID-19. Finn would not be able to go to the Galápagos Islands but insisted that Diana go by herself. He wanted her to be out of the city and somewhere safe where she would not get the virus. Reluctantly, Diana finally gave in and traveled to Galapagos alone. As soon as Diana arrived at the airport on Galapagos, she was greeted with the information that her luggage was lost. She decided to take the ferry to Isabela where she and Finn had booked a room at one of the hotels. Just as the ferry docked, Diana was given the choice to return to the mainland. Isabela was under quarantine and almost everything was shut down. For some unknown reason, Diana decided to stay. She was about to find out that the hotel where she had a reservation was shut down. Diana had no luggage and nowhere to stay. Abuela, one of the women that cleaned the hotel took pity on her. Through hand gestures and the little bit of Spanish Diana could muster, she asked Abuela if she knew anyplace where she could stay. Abuela took Diana under her wing and offered her a place to stay. It was also almost impossible to get a message to Finn. The Wi-Fi on the island was almost nonexistent. As time passed on the island, Diana discovered its hidden treasures and beauty and was trusted with Beatriz’s secret and the special bond she formed with Gabriel. Diana began to wonder if this was the life she was meant to live rather than the one that waited for her back home in New York. In Jodi Picoult’s author’s note, she conveyed the idea where she got the idea for writing this book. “Several months into the pandemic I stumbled across an article about a Japanese man who got stranded in Machu Picchu during COVID. He was trapped there due to travel restrictions and, out of necessity, stopped being a tourist and became a resident of the community. That was Jodi Picoult’s spring board for writing Wish You Were Here. In my opinion, I believe that this was one of her best novels to date if not her absolute best one. She gathered her research by interviewing medical professionals and survivors who had been on ventilators. Even though I lived through and am still living through the consequences, precautions and challenges of COVID-19 I was reminded of how this virus has changed our life as it was once was. Having two daughters and a son-in-law in the medical field, I was extremely cautious and still am as I always worried for their safety and health and mine. I devoured Wish You Were Here. The characters were so believable and memorable. I felt like I really knew them by the end of the book. It made me smile and even shed a few tears at parts of the story. I highly recommend this book. Diana’s life is going along exactly as planned. She’s certain that her boyfriend, a surgical resident, will propose to her on their trip to the Galapagos islands. Diana O’Toole’s life is working out just the way she planned. Diana is the primary narrator of the novel, but we get to hear Finn’s tragic side of things when he sends email to Diana from the New York City hospital where he works. Abandoned in Death by J. D. Robb (pseudonym for Nora Roberts) brings murder, romance and suspense to a well-written futuristic police procedural set mainly in New York City. This novel has a slightly different format for this series in that it alternates timelines between the early part of the twenty-first century and June of 2061. What happens when the past and the present collide? Our protagonist, Lieutenant Eve Dallas of the NYC police department, arrives at a crime scene at a playground near friends Mavis and Leonardo’s new house. Joined by her partner, Detective Delia Peabody, they find the body of a young woman with vintage make-up, hair, and clothing and a note written in crayon saying “Bad Mommy”. With clues pointing to an older antagonist and no records of crimes with a similar MO, how will Eve, Delia, and the team solve the crime? Learning that other young women have recently vanished, they know they need to solve this case quickly. Time spent with Eve, her husband Roarke, and Eve’s colleagues is always entertaining. Eve is definitely a compelling and three-dimensional character. Her need to serve and protect comes through in every book, but the underlying impetus for this is best understood by reading this series in order. Due to the way Eve was raised, she often doesn’t understand commonly used phrases and this comes into play a few times in this book making her seem more real and less perfect. As always, the interactions between Eve and Roarke are enjoyable and bring a different facet of Eve’s personality to light. Many of the reoccurring police characters play significant roles in this book. In addition, readers also get to see a bit of their private lives. I especially enjoyed seeing the character development of intern Jamie Lingstrom. Additionally, I was delighted to see a different side of Detective Jenkinson near the end of the book. As always, Dr. Mira’s psychological profiling, Morris’ autopsy results, and Roarke’s computer skills, as well as Eve and Delia’s efforts, work against time to solve the case. The writing is fluid and flows well. The prose is suspenseful and engrossing in this intense race against the clock. A thought-provoking, stunning, deeply involved, and tragic plot gripped this reader immediately. It is appalling in places and uplifting in others. Will you guess the identity of the killer? This one was a surprise to me. As always, the interview segment near the end of the story is compelling. Seeing Eve and Delia working it together with Dr. Mira added another dimension to it. Robb manages to embed humor in her novels, providing some much needed levity to offset some of the more serious and grim aspects of the story. She brings strong characters, great plots, wonderful relationships, and excellent pacing to this series. Themes include murder, justice, and family dynamics, as well as standing up for the innocent and the dead. If you enjoy engaging near-future police procedurals with some romance and humor, then I recommend this series. This is the fifty-third book in the In Death Eve Dallas series and I have read all of them up to this point. Overall, it is entertaining, and over time, it is like spending time with old friends. I can’t wait to read the next book in the series. Opinions expressed in this review are completely my own and are not biased in any way. Publication date was February 8, 2022. Actual rating: 4.5 stars, rounded up. Abandoned in Death is the 54th installment in Nora Roberts’ In Death series, penned under the pseudonym J.D. Robb. For a while there I though that Nora might have been running out of ideas for this series and was just keeping it going for the sake of the characters, but it turns out those few weaker installments were outliers, not indicative of the new norm. This book and the two before it were all stronger in plot, while still providing a chance to visit with characters who have become so solid over the course of more than 50 novels that they nearly jump off the page when you crack the books open. In this installment, Nora plays with time and perspective more than usual for the series, which was a fun and interesting change. These elements provided not only additional insight, but more emotional investment in the outcome. While Eve always solves the case in the end, in this book I was on the edge of my seat hoping that she would do so before the other perspective in the present timeline was killed. I enjoyed the added tension in what was already a very interesting, nuanced case. Of course, my favorite element of Abandoned in Death was, as always, catching up with Eve and Roarke and Peabody and the rest. These characters feel so incredibly real to me. I’ve known them since my teen years and have loved watching them grow and change and embark on new phases of life. You would think that, after 54 books, even the best of characters would feel stale, their interactions repetitive. But that’s not the case for this series, at least for me. Just like getting to see the people who matter to me in real life always brings me joy, so does getting to catch up with these characters. And Eve’s bafflement over common idioms always makes me laugh. If you’ve never read anything by Nora and are a lover of both police procedurals and incredible character development, I urge you to pick up the first book in this series, Naked in Death. They’re truly worthwhile reads, and you’ll get a highly unconventional found family in the process.

I enjoyed this, the 25th installment of the series featuring my all-time favorite male character in a book series more, I believe, than any of the 24 that came before it - and as far as I know, I haven't missed a single one. I'll admit I read it following a book that had so many grammatical and content errors that I can't believe it got past publishing house editors, and perhaps that did influence my appreciation of this one a bit. In any event, the contrast really underscored how wonderful it is to read a story that's well-written, engrossing and entertaining. And for sure this one is all that and more. Even though the star of the show, Gabriel Allon, no longer officially plies his trade as a well-known and successful Mossad spy, his legend continues. These days, he practices his unmatched talent as a restorer of art (not only does he "fix" damaged artwork by the old masters, he can copy their style so well that experts can't tell his painting isn't an original). As he and his beautiful wife Chiara and their twins Raphael and Irene live the good life, he's been working on the restoration of a very important one. That work gets rudely interrupted, however, with his discovery of a dead woman in the waters of the Venetian Lagoon. That, in turn, leads him inside the walls of the Vatican, where a painting thought to be a lost DaVinci - which could be worth many millions of dollars - somehow disappeared. Soon it's clear that the painting could not have gone missing without help from the inside. Since Gabriel is good friends with the Pope (he played an instrumental role in his election, in fact), the two meet up quite often. Mind you, I'm not Catholic, but I loved the late Pope Francis and the current Pope Leo XIV). Gabriel's good buddy, though, turns out to be an absolute delight - every interaction between the two brought a smile to my face (despite concern that either or both will make it out of the book alive). The rest of the story, of course, serves up details on how they plan to get the painting back, what really happened to the dead woman and who the bad guys and gals are. It's the usual suspense and action, but also to my great delight it brings together several familiar characters from previous books and puts a bit brighter spotlight on Gabriel's delightful 9-year-olds. All good things must come to an end, of course, and already I'm chomping at the bit for the next adventure. After all these years, Gabriel may be getting a little long in the tooth and tries his best to avoid the kind of dangerous cloak-and-dagger situations that earned him his stellar reputation as a spy. But he certainly hasn't lost his edge - if anything, he's just become all the more interesting.

Daniel Silva shows prowess with this latest and perhaps last, installment of the Gabriel Allon series. And it stands apart from the rest since our hero has retired from Israeli intelligence and works exclusively as an art restoration expert specializing in masterworks from the fifteenth century. We find him and his family back in Venice where he's in the process of yet another restoration. When a woman's body is found floating in a canal, we're off to the races. Silva uses a reunion of characters from past installments here; among them Luigi Donati, who was elected Pope, Sarah Bankcroft, Christopher Keller, Julian Isherwood and countless others. When its determined the deceased woman had been working at the Vatican to restore an unknown DaVinci panel, the mystery kicks into high gear. Since Allon has a personal relationship with Donati, he's summoned to the Vatican to investigate. With each chapter we learn of unscrupulous characters of which several are high ranking Vatican members. Cardinal Bertoli becomes a target having invested the Vatican's funds in real estate, and secured the loan with the unknown Leonardo as collateral; worse yet, the lender is a corrupt bank owned by the Camorra, aka Italian mob. In past installments we learned about Gabriel's ability to expertly forge works of art. However, this is an unknown DaVinci painted on a walnut panel in 1490! Since Donati is well aware of his former spy friend's ability to find culprits and solve mystery, he stands on the sidelines while the master goes to work! Complexity, unique premise and plot twists are what we expect from Mr. Silva and we experience this many times over. Additionally we receive education of Leonardo, masterpiece restoration, forging techniques and so much more. In other words, this is storytelling at its best. Put simply this is the most unique chapter in the series, yet compelling nonetheless. And at first I thought the lack of The Office team might diminish its impact but Silva manages to overcome their absence in spades. As always, I feel revealing plot points and twists spoil reader experience. That said, fans of masterpiece artworks, intrigue and mystery will enjoy this from start to finish.

Book Review An Inside Job Daniel Silva reviewed by Lou Jacobs readersremains.com | Goodreads Daniel Silva superbly reprises the twenty-fifth adventure of the iconic Israeli intelligence officer and sometime assassin, Gabriel Allon. His cover story has always involved his supreme talent as an art restorer, a trade he now plies full-time in his beloved Venice. He resides there with his beautiful wife, Chiara, and their adored twins, Raphael and Irene. Gabriel has been tenaciously working to restore Titian’s The Descent of the Holy Spirit to its natural beauty. During a coffee break while strolling along the Venetian Lagoon, he notices the body of a young woman floating face down. The Italian police are unable to identify her and request Gabriel’s help in creating a forensic sketch of her face based on her skull X-rays and disfigured features. The murdered woman is soon identified as an American, Penelope Radcliff, who recently completed her art conservator apprenticeship at the Vatican Museum. Gabriel immediately suspects a connection between her murder and her recent studies at the Vatican. The pope, His Holiness Luigi Donati, and Gabriel share a deep and trusted friendship forged through Gabriel’s help in several previous sensitive matters. Gabriel is granted permission to initiate a discreet investigation, which soon reveals that an unreported painting is missing from the Vatican storerooms. He surmises this occurred during a suspicious blackout, coinciding with a visit from a mysterious “priest.” Penelope had reported to her superiors that she suspected a prestigious painting was buried beneath a lackluster Madonna and Child, likely the work of a Raphael imitator. She believed it was a “lost” Leonardo da Vinci. Giorgio Montefiore, a “Leonardo” expert, assessed the painting and cast doubt on its provenance—though he privately suspected it was the real thing. His greed set in motion a criminal conspiracy that led to the murder of not only Penelope but also Montefiore. Caught in this web of deceit is the nefarious Cardinal Matteo Bertoli, the sostituto responsible for the Vatican’s financial affairs, and his corrupt dealings with illicit bankers and financiers. All paths ultimately lead to the notorious criminal organization known as the Camorra and its Swiss banking arm, which launders vast sums of money. Gabriel must construct a complex plan with multiple moving parts to recover the painting before it is sold and lost forever. This endeavor calls for the help of many of his beloved associates, who admirably reprise their roles in this intricate plot. Daniel Silva proves once again to be a masterful storyteller as he weaves multiple plotlines together with escalating tension and intrigue. He explores, with no holds barred, the often-corrupt financial dealings of the Vatican and the dark underbelly of the art world. The FBI has documented that 90 percent of all museum heists involve an inside component. This fictional account evokes memories of real historical scandals—such as that of Cardinal Giovanni Becciu, who was convicted of embezzlement and fraud in 2023. Silva’s denouement explodes with a barrage of bullets that endanger multiple key players in St. Peter’s Square. He remains a master of international intrigue and suspense. Thanks to HarperCollins Publishers for providing an advance copy of this gem in exchange for an honest review. Already looking forward to his twenty-sixth novel .... Daniel Silva once again reminds readers why he’s one of the most gifted novelists of our time with his latest must-read thriller, The Order. It was supposed to be a vacation. A badly needed, week-long trip to relax and recharge. And after years of dedicated service that has no doubt taken a major toll on him and his family, nobody needed it more than Gabriel Allon, the master art restorer turned Israeli assassin who’s now halfway into his first term as chief of the Office. However, just one day into his holiday—a covert trip to Venice with his family, arranged by his wife, Chiara—an old friend urgently requests Gabriel’s help. Pope Paul VII has died. News reports suggest the leader of the Catholic church passed away from a massive heart attack that occurred while he was praying in his favorite chapel. But Archbishop Luigi Donati, the Holy Father’s loyal private secretary, suspects there might just be more to the story than anyone else is letting on, and in order to find out for sure, he sends for Gabriel Allon. Another key person is German Jonas Wolf owner of the multibillion-dollar (euro) empire called The Wolf Group that funds the Order. Author Freida McFadden explores the potentially dangerous pitfalls of online dating through the eyes of women of a certain age who have suffered one too many disastrous dates while looking for Mr. Perfect in her latest book, THE BOYFRIEND. Wasting no time, McFadden sets a chilling, ominous tone in the Prologue - a clear forewarning of the danger lurking at every turn, on every page, in her latest psychological thriller. Sydney Shaw is knocking hard on the door of thirty-five, her biological clock ticking loudly, counting down the days with no viable lifetime partner possibilities on the horizon. Her latest obnoxious online date is yet another disaster, and she can't wait to cut the tortuous evening short. When he refuses to accept an emphatic no to walking her home, Sydney follows her gut taking him down the wrong street to "her house" where he suddenly turns from annoying to violent. Having seen no one in the surrounding area, Sydney is surprised but relieved when a dark, handsome stranger sends her attacker scurrying, but before she can get his name, he melts back into the shadows from whence he came. In the weeks to come, Sydney becomes obsessed with finding the dark-haired stranger until finally he's there - her hero seducing her with his good looks, charming smile and hypnotic words. Sydney's convinced this man may be the one even though some of the things he's telling her doesn't add up. Has her luck finally changed? Or is his perfection a mask? Meantime, police are investigating a string of unsolved murders believed to have been committed by an unknown man the women connected with through online dating. When tragedy hits close to home, Sydney's suspicions run rampant as she begins questioning the small inconsistencies in her new boyfriend's story. Has Sydney found the perfect man . . . or the perfect killer? THE BOYFRIEND is an intense, immersive thriller that is rendered through dual timelines and alternating points of view which are highly effective in allowing readers to learn firsthand how certain players got to the current point in the story. McFadden brilliantly maneuvers characters and readers through a complex plot line that keeps shifting and twisting at an ever-increasing pace before finally dropping a last minute, shocking bombshell that left this reader reeling. The author's ability to misdirect readers with several vexing red herrings raises the stakes, leaving them guessing. Authentic characterizations make it easy to feel empathy for some while making it difficult to discover who's being truthful and who's manipulative, carefully hidden beneath a mask. A suffocating air of malice thickens page by page, leaving little doubt danger is nigh. Author Freida McFadden gifts readers with another gripping, page turner thriller in THE BOYFRIEND. In doing so, she shines a spotlight on the danger of online dating and the real possibility of evil lurking behind carefully constructed facades. Themes of obsession, stalking, loneliness, seduction, and the suggestive public's perception of women, especially of a certain age, are explored. Fans of this author's work are sure to love this one! Also highly recommended to fans of twisted psychological thrillers with last page shockers. Nicholas Sparks’ new novel, “Dreamland”, is reminiscent of both “Dear John” and “Safe Haven” (both Sparks’ novels I thoroughly enjoyed), however it is also entirely unique in its own right. In true Sparks fashion, Colby and Morgan are from entirely different backgrounds and upbringings, yet manage to connect with each other through their love of music. Add to that the information on organic farming that Sparks peppers throughout the novel, and “Dreamland” became entertaining and informative! I know there will be a movie or Netflix adaptation forthcoming, as is the case with most Sparks novels, and I would be intrigued to see how it plays out onscreen. CHOSEN FAMILY TROPE I’m a sucker for this trope, it’s on my top 3 favorite tropes ever. Almost all my favorite books portrait a chosen family. And Maas is really great at developing this trope. I’m just mad this book’s chosen family consisted on Bryce and other 8 dudes. One of them was her mate. Another was her BFF who had secretly had a crush on her for forever. Another was gay. And lastly, her fake-fiance and new character who ended up adding nothing to the plot, but okay. Are you seeing what I’m seeing? Maas surrounded Bryce in a garden of peens. Not only that, but several of these dudes openly lusted after her. Where are the female friends??? Remember she had two in the previous book? Anyone remembers Hypaxia? She didn’t even show up in the story until past the half mark. And sure, she tentatively joined the group, but it wasn’t the same as the others. Like, wtf is up with that? I’m not vibing with this shit, let me be real here. And sadly, I think it has something to do with my next point. LGBTI REPRESENTATION Oh my god. OH MY FUCKING GOD. I’m livid, y’all. I’m so angry and disappointed and frustrated and just—What the fuck, Maas??? Alright, let’s compare couples so it’s obvious where the problem is. There are 3 queer couples in this book. 1. Declan and his boyfriend Marc. They started dating in between CC1 and CC2 so we don’t get to see any of this. Marc is just there and Bryce explains briefly they’ve been dating for a month and that’s it. They don’t touch or have any type of intimate moment throughout the whole book. Not even once. There's nothing to indicate they're romantically involved. No chemistry or sexual tension between them. So what, are we expected to care about them??? Sarah J Maas surely didn’t. She didn’t even bother to throw us a bone to pick our interest. The worst part is that Marc shows up only when they need his legal advice, since he’s a lawyer. So it feels like the character was only created to help move forward the plot. He has no agency or really any type of personality, except for being there and saying a few lines related to laws. 2. Juniper and Fury. Their romance shows up a little bit more. The book starts with them happily living together. So there’s no tension or anything that could pick the reader’s interest there. Their romance is just done and over. At least they kiss once, I guess. They are barely in the story, even though they’re supposedly Bryce’s best friends. I’m just mad because the chosen family trope was so well done in this book but it was Bryce and 8 other dudes. All the female characters disappeared or barely showed up at all during the book. And sadly, Juniper and Fury suffered the consequences. So why should I care about them? If I never got to read how their romance happened and I don’t get to read about them now either. 3. Celestine and Hypaxia. Which was a really good plot twist, let me add. Our love is stronger than time, greater than any distance. Our love spans across stars and worlds. I will find you again, I promise. House of Sky and Breath is a masterful continuation of the Crescent City series, delivering a complex and gripping narrative that keeps you hooked from beginning to end. This book picks up a few months after the events of "House of Earth and Blood," with Bryce and Hunt laying low on orders from the Asteri Rigelus. Their romance is blossoming, and Bryce is coming to terms with her newfound status as a Starborn Fae Princess with the power of Starlight. The story takes an intriguing turn as Bryce is suddenly betrothed to the Avallar Fae Prince Cormac, a move driven by political motives and her fear of her tyrannical father, the Autumn King. Meanwhile, the mystery of the missing human siblings, Sofie and Emile, unfolds. These siblings may hold a powerful secret related to their ability to control electricity, making them essential in the ongoing human-led Ophion rebellion against the Asteri. The narrative introduces a host of new and fascinating characters, each with their own unique backstories and motivations. As you follow Bryce and Hunt's journey, you'll also become engrossed in the unfolding Ophion rebellion, the complexities of Fae politics, and the profound secrets hidden within the Asteri Archives. The revelations about the Asteri's true nature and their exploitation of worlds add depth to the story, challenging the characters' understanding of the world they inhabit. Throughout the book, the chemistry between Bryce and Hunt deepens, and they come to realize the significance of their bond as mates, a concept in Fae culture that goes beyond traditional marriage. Their relationship is both passionate and tender, making their characters all the more engaging. Sarah J. Maas weaves a rich and intricate tapestry of storytelling, blending romance, action, political intrigue, and revelations about the nature of their world. House of Sky and Breath also leaves readers with a tantalizing cliffhanger, leaving you eager for the next chapter in this spellbinding series. In conclusion, House of Sky and Breath is an enthralling continuation of the Crescent City series that will keep fans of fantasy and romance eagerly turning the pages. It's a must-read for those who appreciate complex world-building, well-developed characters, and a story that never loses its momentum.

But would their strong will and courage be enough to save both Aretia and Xaden? ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ‍‍‍‍‍‍˗ˏˋ★‿︵‧ ˚ ₊⊹ honest thoughts ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ⋅ ☾ I will first address one of the most controversial aspects of this work, which is its slow pace. I want to make it clear that this is completely a personal opinion, but I loved the way the action moved in this book, and I definitely appreciated all the new information. ㅤ While I enjoy action-packed books that keep me really intrigued, I love it when a series, especially one with more than three books, simply slows things down a bit and works on strengthening relationships between characters and historical aspects of the book; all while bringing new information to put my mind to work. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ⋅ ☾ And, following what I mentioned above, I also want to talk about the supposed information dump in this book. Is there a lot of information for you to process in this book? Yes, A LOT, and I might genuinely need a second reading to be able to notice the things I clearly missed at first. But for me, nothing from this book seemed too much or too overwhelming in terms of new information. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍I am the type of person that seeks out all conceivable information in a book series, so if you take political, historical, and sociological aspects of a fictional world and accurately present them in a book, I will devour each piece of it. This series is simply my guilty pleasure. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ⋅ ☾ Another thing I saw mentioned a lot about this book is how this just entirely feels like a filler book. And while I do see where everyone is coming from and I can understand why so many people were disappointed by this, this series just thrived with this book, in my humble opinion. Once again, this is only my personal taste because I love a good filler book when it is placed at the perfect moment in a series. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ I think I became bored of trying to keep up with all the action scenes in the first two novels since the events were so fast-paced and dramatic. So you can understand why a much slower novel that focusses on introducing new information while also shining a light on many side characters was so enjoyable for me. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ⋅ ☾ This book is exhausting to read and I am not even kidding with this. I had to read it while continually switching between checking who is who and locating what they are talking about on the map. But I would be a complete hypocrite to state that I was so impacted by this in such a way that it took away the pleasure of reading for me, especially since at one point I had to do the same for Throne of Glass, which is my favourite series ever. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ⋅ ☾ This is honestly my favourite version of Xaden and Violet so far. Many people commented on how odd Xaden and Violet's actions were in this novel. To be honest, in Xaden's situation, I suppose that was to be expected, as well as purposeful, given that he isn't totally himself. However, both characters seemed grown while still maintaining the "madly in love" component. I got to see a badass Violet who has finally stopped doubting herself at every turn, as well as a Xaden who borders on insanity more than once, and they both worked for me. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ⋅ ☾ Lastly, the romance in this book was just so perfect for me that I was shocked how much I am enjoying it at one point. After the cringe show that Fourth Wing was for me and the therapeutic approach to romance that Iron Flame brought, this was like a breath of fresh air. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ Illogical longing? Angst? With a sprinkle of completely uncalled for drama at times? Yes, please. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ⋅ ☾ The ending was absolutely perfect for me. Go ahead, break my heart and right after that also make my brain struggle and I will surely absolutely love that ending. I am a only person that simply loves to suffer in uncertainty. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ‍‍‍‍‍‍˗ˏˋ★‿︵‧ ˚ ₊⊹ characters ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍I feel like I have so much to say about these characters that I can't find the perfect words. So, I'll try to limit myself to as little information as possible while yet covering all of the key points. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ⚔︎ Violet - If you saw me commenting on both Fourth Wing and Iron Flame you know that I always had a love-hate relationship with her as a character. I can genuinely say that this book, finally, made me like Violet a bit more and find her slightly more relatable as a character. It is evident that she has finally found her centre, and she flourishes here. Despite all of the setbacks and things that appear to go against all of her intentions, she never gives up and keeps trying. I loved seeing that she was no longer destroyed by failure, and it was very motivating on some level. She still had a long way to go for me to genuinely appreciate her as a character, but so far, she appears to be on the right track. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ⚔︎ Xaden - I am weak; you give me a hopeless, miserable, lost and yet frighteningly strong tortured soul, and I will simply fold in an instant. He wasn't the same character we met in the previous two books? Fine. Perfect, even! That's because he wasn't even supposed to be the Xaden we met in the previous two books and this was perefectly shown here. You all know the ending of Iron Flame and what it implied; you all know that once someone channels, they slowly start to lose more and more of themselves to the power. So why did anyone expect to not see any changes in Xaden? Of course, he was going to be different and, apparently, this type of "different" just worked perfectly for me. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ I suffer from the I can change him syndrome, so of course an unhinged, slightly mad and insane at times Xaden was enough to make me swoon. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ⚔︎ Tairn, Andarna, Sgaeyl - I love them. I simply love all the dragons. But Tairn will always have a special place in my heart, and I don't think I will ever be able to get over what an amazing character he is in this book AGAIN. He is just perfect, he has no flaws. He would probably rip my head off for it, but I badly want to pet him and tell him I live for his sassiness. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ⚔︎ Ridoc ♡ - Is he my favurite character in this book? ABSOLUTELY. I already fell in love with him and all his shenanigans since Fourth Wing, but the fact that he got so much attention in this book was the best thing that could have happened. We were already used to his jokes and his role of our comic relief, but the caring and protective side of him and his loyalty that simply shines in this book are unmatched. I feared for his life throughout the entire book, and I will never forgive Rebecca for that heart attack I almost had. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ⚔︎ Mira and Brennan - I might still not entirely trust any of them, but they really do care about Violet and I really hope they manage to overcome whatever family drama they are currently experiencing. I love them as siblings; they are the perfect example of how siblings actually act at times, and I badly need nothing to happen to any of them. I am still highly annoyed by their unnecessary drama at times, but I guess this is their way of progressing. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ⚔︎ Garrick, Bodhi and Imogen - I am putting these three together because the loyalty they have and the pure devotion to Xaden and, surprisingly, to Violet's protection is simply beautiful. I am really begging Rebecca to give us more of them. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ⚔︎ Sawyer, Rhiannon, Dain, Sloane, Cat, Aaric, Maren - Nothing will ever make me stop loving our lovely squad. I would badly love to talk more about them, especially Sawyer's progress and Aaric's shocking and incredibly amazing development, but this is unfortunately already getting too lengthy; and I promised myself to not reach the word limit like I did with my review for Iron Flame once again. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ What I do want to mention here, however, is that I need Rebecca to understand that not any small and insignificat character in this book needs a name. Lucky for me, I didn't really mind going back and forth and listening to so many new names being added to the characters list. But I totally see how some readers might feel so overwhelmed by this. I am perfectly ok with knowing there is "a general/ a liutenant/ a rider/ a flier/ whatever else there is". I don't need to know their name, history and family. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ‍‍‍‍‍‍˗ˏˋ★‿︵‧ ˚ ₊⊹ should you read this? ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ I am a straightforward person with honest remarks, therefore I will simply ask you: Did you enjoy the first two volumes in this series? If the answer is yes, then give it a shot. You may like or loathe it, but you should surely read it. But if the answer is no, what exactly are you doing here? I mean, unless you want to turn this into a hate read, in which case I completely understand and support you.God knows how many hate reads I have done in my life, so I won't be anyone's moral compass. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ‍‍‍‍‍‍I devoured this book. I was unable to put it down and it had me entirely hooked from page one. I understand that various readers look for different things when determining if a book is excellent or poor, but I am primarily a mood reader, and all that counts to me in a book is how it made me feel. If I have true fun while reading it, if I cry or laugh with the characters, and if the book itself manages to make me sympathise with what it is attempting to convey, I don't need anything else to rate it; I have all I need right there. Not to add that the ending was completely mind-blowing in ways I can't even begin to articulate. I loved the cliffhanger and the confusion it created. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ‍‍‍‍‍‍So, unexpectedly enough even for me, Onyx Storm is my first 5-star read of 2025. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ‍‍‍‍‍‍˗ˏˋ★‿︵‧ ˚ ₊⊹ ❗ Theories - spoilers ahead ❗ ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ ‍‍‍‍‍‍I generally do not do this in my reviews, but my mind is working fast right now and I just needed to express these thoughts somewhere. Who desired dragon eggs in exchange for military assistance? Queen of Unnbriel. Who was the primary translator of their language and the sole royal representative? Aaric. And who is a distance wielder who can bring Aaric and the eggs there faster? Garrick. This is simply my guess. ㅤ ‍‍‍‍‍‍ - Despite the angst, I believe Imogen's decision to erase Violet's memory was completely essential. Violet cannot know Xaden's location in case she is investigated for this. ”’What did you do?’ ‘What you asked me to.’” ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ ★ The biggest f-ing 6 stars, gosh maybe the best book of the series (but I said that about both prior books) ⚔️This review will be rant first, review second. You can skip the rant if you want! I have to defend this series ON MY HONOR.⚔️ I feel like it needs to be said that Yarros very clearly after Fourth Wing decided to take this from a fun romantasy into a more serious epic high fantasy - so if that isn’t your jam, I wouldn’t recommend this book or series to you. There’s a lot of world-building, an overarching plot with multiple side plots, multiple enemies, sprinklings of foreshadowing throughout that you need to remember, and many new characters — this is how epic high fantasy goes. I know that’s not how it started, but it’s how it’s going and continuing to evolve, so if you don’t enjoy that, just hop off the train. You are allowed to not enjoy books and have your own opinion, but also why waste your precious time reading books of a genre you don’t enjoy and then hate on it, you know? High fantasy takes a lot of effort and critical thinking to understand if you want to really enjoy what the author is trying to do. You are allowed to stop reading a series if you aren’t enjoying it. With that - what’s up with all the hate reads? What’s the point? That doesn’t seem like a fair assessment of a book when you had the pretense of hating it. Why is this a thing? You don’t buy a piece of clothing that you hate and obviously isn’t your style, wasting your hard-earned money and the hours you spent making said money, and then go and review it saying it’s the ugliest thing you’ve ever owned and give it 1 star, right? If you want to lose hours of your life doing a hate read, fine I guess. But if you go in with the idea that you’re going to hate it and hate it the whole time, maybe don’t give it a star rating. It just unnecessarily skews the ratings for people who are actually looking for a new book or series to enjoy. Books change lives. This series changed my life. I went through something terrible, and this book/series and these characters got me through it. You might think that’s stupid, and that’s fine, but it was exactly what I needed when I read it. THIS SERIES MIGHT BE EXACTLY WHAT SOMEONE NEEDS RIGHT NOW BUT THEY WONT PICK IT UP BECAUSE THEY SEE A BUNCH OF 1 STAR HATE REVIEWS. *There’s a difference between going in excited/neutral reading a book and not liking it, and just hating it the whole time and never giving it a chance. Let’s stop wasting the precious hours of our lives hate reading, and set on your mission to find your next life-altering book. *RANT OVER* ⋆༺𓆩⚔𓆪༻⋆ ⋆༺𓆩⚔𓆪༻⋆ ⋆༺𓆩⚔𓆪༻⋆ *ENTER REVIEW* ‼️SPOILERS AHEAD‼️ buckle in folks, it’s gonna be a long one🫡 I can’t say how impressed I am with this book. I felt like Iron Flame definitely took the necessary steps to get us where we are at, and I am so down for it. Shifting into high fantasy mode.✨ Onyx Storm is absolutely epic. I would say that we are out of our easy to read Fourth Wing era, and have entered our critical reading era. I think if you read this book just like you would any other, it would be an okay read. However, if you do a literary analysis while you are reading, being sure to pick up on the careful wording, the foreshadowing planted throughout, etc - you will find yourself reading an excellently executed book. Yarros did not. miss. a. beat. While I was reading it felt like I was attempting to solve a puzzle the whole time, trying to put together the pieces Yarros was giving us, and it was so exciting. Basically, if you love epic high fantasy, this book is for you. ⋆༺𓆩⚔𓆪༻⋆ ⋆༺𓆩⚔𓆪༻⋆ ⋆༺𓆩⚔𓆪༻⋆ ”’You need to be able to find me.’ ‘Why me? Xaden!’ ‘Because you’re the only one capable of killing me.’” ⚔️Plot: Talk about an incredible plot. There is still the overarching plot of the war with the venin, but we have multiple side plots that are characteristic of high fantasy. Violet is trying to find the irids while also attempting to discover a cure for the venin, Xaden is trying to keep himself from turning initiate to asim, also while being Duke of Tyrrendor, PROFESSOR RIORSON 🥵, fighting battles, and also holding more of his own secrets. THE POLITICAL INTRIGUE. Gosh I am such a sucker for politics in fantasy books, so naturally I loved the Senarium/Assembly. And mostly, I enjoyed Xaden stomping down everyone else’s peasant ideas. The quest squad might just be one of my favourite developments of this book. Without even discussing character development during this sequence of Onyx Storm - THE WORLD BUILDING. We literally get to discover like 5 different locations while they are trying to secure alliances. Each place was so rich with its own culture; I think Deverelli was my absolute favourite. *I can’t wait to see if the compass leads Violet to Xaden* The finale of this book was exceptional; there was so much to dissect and put away for later. The Nature Valley granola bar was crumbing all over the place. It truly was an incredible ending. Did she channel? Did Theophanie tell Violet the cure? Is Andarna back? Was that Imogen’s second signet? Is Garrick the new “brother”? ⚔️Characters: Well, Yarros really knows how to get us invested, I don’t know what else to say. I’m obsessed with second squad. Rhi is an excellent leader, and thank god SOMEONE is capable of forgiving secrets around here. I really appreciated the growth we get from Sawyer in this book, and how he faces his own physical battles. I thought it was *chef’s kiss* that he wanted Violet to be the one out there when he tried mounting. Lastly…do we even need to discuss Ridoc? He carried in this book. Not only is he the funniest and wittiest [enter making fun of Vi and Xaden’s arguments], but we get to see an incredibly protective side of him that warms your heart. I hate to say this with every fiber of my being…but she’s gotten us too attached to this side character. You know what that means. 🥺 I adore Cat so much in this book, which is something I wouldn’t have been able to say when we met her, but the arc is definitely there in Iron Flame. I was so happy to see her in a relationship…but I don’t think I can go there. I’m still in shock. ”Thank you.” NAH you can 🖕🏻 off Rebecca. I also adore Aaric, and Sloane, and Bodhi. Aaric just wants to be helpful, and then he manifests the most useful signet. He’s so cool. 🖤Xaden: I was completely down and heartbroken for his character arc in this book. Talk about Anakin in Revenge of the Sith vibes. Xaden is my guy, and somehow I was simultaneously devastated and thrilled every time he channeled. It was incredible to see the power he had at the end of the book. PROFESSOR RIORSON WILL NEVER LEAVE MY MIND. Duke!? Married to Violet!? Slamming Halden into the wall? And the way he just took down every single student at Basgaith on the mat without even moving? I don’t care what anyone says, his shadows matched with his inntinsic ability makes him the most powerful person. And I totally knew he saw Violet eyeing that silk in Deverelli…my heart🥺 💤Violet’s second signet…dare I say underwhelmed? I’m sure it’ll have a true purpose in the next books, but for now I’m not too impressed. Also, everyone developing second signets makes it not feel as special or incredible that Xaden had a second signet. I think it’s related to this quote, but still. ”The rarest of signets—those that rise once in a generation or century—have manifested concurrently with an equal twice in our records, both critical times in our history, but only once have the six most powerful walked the Continent simultaneously.” 🐲Dragons: The wit. The sarcasm. This book was even better with the dragon banter. Tairn is a top tier character for me; I love how he is exactly what Violet needs. Andarna…can I even talk about this? Caught me off guard big time. The way she just…left and came back, I don’t know what to make of it. I think Yarros has executed the romance/relationship progression through this series perfectly. The first book we get to see their obvious chemistry. This is to get everyone invested in them (which it does). The second book they obviously have to spend more time apart and they go through their frustrating phases of very poor communication - but ultimately they work things out and do much better. I think this is all exactly for this book, when Xaden is venin. They have to be able to be truthful and trusting of one another with his new power (although they still kept secrets but I mean, I think it’s time we stop expecting them to not). It’s frustrating to me that everyone is saying “what romance?” in Onyx Storm. Romance isn’t just breaking armoires and setting buildings on fire - it doesn’t always have to be about sex. With that being said, I honestly thought we got more scenes with the two of them than I anticipated after the Iron Flame finale. This book is showing us why they are meant to be together beyond the physical attraction and how they are willing to do anything to fight for one another, as well as the maturity that they developed that their relationship lacked in the prior books. I think this book is to make us BELIEVE that. Xaden says that Violet is who he serves above Tyrrendor, above Nevarre, and I believe it. I believe he means it. I don’t think he can be so far gone that he’d ever forget Violet. ”My loyalty is to Violet first above everything, everyone else.” ⋆༺𓆩⚔𓆪༻⋆ ⋆༺𓆩⚔𓆪༻⋆ ⋆༺𓆩⚔𓆪༻⋆ Also, please stop saying the loose ends are a cash grab; it’s literally a plot device. We aren’t supposed to feel like the book has been wrapped in a big bow before the final one; we are supposed to be left waiting and anticipating. All authors do this - it’s how you keep readers coming back to your series. I do have to say, despite how much I adore this series and loved this book, I don’t understand how there can be two more books. I just simply don’t. To me, this book was the equivalent of Empire of Storms in TOG - trying to get the alliances ready before Kingdom of Ash (I don’t count Tower of Dawn lol). Either the next book is a continuation of trying to get alliances and a cure, finding a cure and Xaden gets to come back to us (and him and Violet finally get a book to actually fully be together for the last one), or maybe it’s even a book about Xaden rising through the venin ranks. I don’t know - but I would rather just take one massive book like Kingdom of Ash because I just don’t know how there can be two more books (and I don’t want to wait). TWO. MORE. BOOKS. HOW. Once again no, this doesn’t mean it’s a cash grab; Yarros obviously has a plan. I’m just curious to the direction we are going to go. ⋆༺𓆩⚔𓆪༻⋆ ⋆༺𓆩⚔𓆪༻⋆ ⋆༺𓆩⚔𓆪༻⋆ Okay folks, party’s over. There’s my hot take. One of the best high fantasies I’ve read. How do I leave this world I’ve been living in for 10 days… ————————— too emotional. review tomorrow 🫠

MORE pain?? what did poor xaden do to her i swear 😭 but actually though, i feel like this entire book was just xaden getting beat up again and again and again until things basically became hopeless for him. ngl it feels so unfair because at this point i think bro just deserves a happy ending. i don’t think he can take much more of this. and i’ll be quite upset if he doesnt get some sort of peace in the fourth book because this whole “let’s make this character so tragic everyone is hurting for him” trope is getting real old. anyways, enough with the sad stuff. let’s move on to what really made xaden shine in this book for me: his personality. this entire series, his entire trademark is just being this dark brooding asshole who’s so ruthless he’ll kill you in a second. only violet really knows the softer, kinder soul that he hides behind that armor. that’s really what makes xaden such a good mmc in my eyes—i’m probably just basic asf, but the whole grumpy on the outside but soft on the inside trope does me IN. and seeing xaden finally embrace that side of him and start to relax with people outside violet really warmed my heart. he finally became at peace with himself (for a time, at least), and open to loving, and we really saw him start to improve, almost. i seriously admired his character growth in this book—he almost became a different person, but really, he just healed. she thor ୨୧ aka our resident diva, violet sorrengail. call it controversial, but she’s honestly still one of my favorite fmcs to date. i just love the trope of someone perceived as “weak” or constantly underestimated becomes the most powerful/strongest of them all. violet is such a role model and while she does make questionable choices throughout the series, i love that she has a good heart despite it all. she totally became a leader in this book and it was so heartwarming seeing her mature and step into her potential. she’s so inspirational and i love her. comedic side character TM ୨୧ ugh ridoc gamlyn, my bbg. my boy literally SHINED in this book, his humor is honestly unmatched (and tbh very similar to mine). but i loved that we also got to see his serious side, more of his depth and his character in general. people started taking him seriously for once which i LOVE. he’s probably my favorite character in the entire series, and if he dies? i will RIOT. my pink haired badass ୨୧ imogen cardulo is my literal wife. her pov chapters were EVERYTHING to me. idk guys, there’s just something about pink haired, lethal women that just do something for me. i can’t explain it. my goddess ୨୧ idk if it was just me, but i didn’t like rhiannon’s character in this. it could be that she just wasn’t in this book as much, but i feel like she’s putting leadership over her friends a lot and she’s not really as important. don’t get me wrong, i like her, but she’s not my favorite anymore. that one bitchass ex ୨୧ idc what anyone says, i fucking love her. always have and always will. end of story. the quest squad ୨୧ can i just say i absolutely LOVED their dynamic? their banter and dialogue was honestly my favorite part of the entire book. ꒰ the plot ⊹ new characters ୨୧ all the new characters being introduced was probably my least favorite part about this book. it was so hard to keep things straight, and very early on in the book i just decided to stop trying and let the names blur. i think rebecca is really overestimating her readers’ intelligence because girl, we cannot understand what you’re saying 😭 that being said, most of the characters weren’t even that important in the future, so it wasn’t that much of a big deal to me. new worlds ୨୧ it was so interesting seeing the quest squad venture out into the isles and see us explore new worlds. each isle had something interesting about it and it was so cool to also see the gods come into play a bit. most of this book was just a shit ton of worldbuilding and honestly it read to me as more of an epic fantasy than the fantasy romance that fourth wing was. you can clearly see the turn that the series is taking and where it’s planning to go in the future. ꒰ the romance ⊹ xadenvi ୨୧ incredible. swoonworthy. heartwarming. their love is literally EVERYTHING to me, and i do not understand the hate that they got in this book? yes, they don’t banter as much anymore and their relationship is more mature, but that’s to be expected. things are basically going to shit, and they don’t really have time for that anymore. plus, in my opinion, they’ve passed the whole flirting stage, and it was so nice to see them just be soft with each other the entire book. miradrake ୨୧ i’m literally obsessed with them. their dynamic is soo cute, and when they basically adopted broccoli?? i literally smiled SO hard, you don’t even know. i honestly ship them so hard and if they don’t get together in book four i’m going to be really sad. they deserve each other, honestly—plus their banter is priceless. sloanedain ୨୧ they’re literally the definition of enemies to lovers, dare i say more than xaden and violet? they’re dynamic is so cute, and begrudgingly, i can say that they both redeemed themselves in onyx storm, especially dain. i just think they’re perfect for each other. imogarrick ୨୧ sigh. let me just say…i do love a good slow burn 😉 catrager ୨୧ why. honestly. just why. ihy rebecca. ──────୨ৎ────── ⚔️ ꒰ entirety. you have been warned. ꒱ ⚔️ ꒰ the ending ⊹ oh gods. i knew the ending was going to be heartbreaking, but i definitely wasn’t expecting this. my heart literally breaks for xaden and sgaeyl. they did not deserve this injustice. and xaden giving up his soul for her…i cant anymore y’all 😭 my only hope is that violet and xaden can connect through dreams, so maybe there’s some hope for him left? i’ll just say, if xaden doesn’t end this series with an HEA, i will scream. and throw the book. and contemplate my life. i’ve become way too attached to these characters to watch them all die at the end, PLEASE rebecca. ꒰ favorite spoiler moments ⊹ જ⁀➴ when violet realizes that xaden is a professor જ⁀➴ xaden’s interactions with the quest squad (especially ridoc) જ⁀➴ violet’s second signet the queen and saving xaden like the queen she is જ⁀➴ andarna breaking the bond…what can i say, i love good angst :( જ⁀➴ XADENVI MARRIAGE, although i hate the circumstances that led to it ꒰ quotes ⊹ Legal suspense at its best! We have a corrupt judge that gets tangled in a game of cat and rat. Could he have been found out? After all this time? He is arrogant and worried (with good reason). "For the first time in his life, he felt like he was on the run". Murder here, murder there, seems like everywhere? What is the connection? Someone knows....... a lot! I really enjoyed this one and was reading it simultaneously with Bone Deep, the true crime novel that highlights massive corruption in the legal system which made it seem even more credible. The investigators are on his trail, trying to stay off his deadly list. There are some suspenseful moments and a few nail-biting scenes as they closed in, this made for a fantastic legal thriller! I read the first in this series, but this could be a standalone. If he writes a third, I'll be in line for it. If you enjoy strong female leads, brilliant characterization, twisty "gotcha" moments and the behind the scenes hunt for a creepy psychopath, you may enjoy it as much as I did. Own a copy/ Feb 2022

What can I say about John Grisham that hasn't already been said a hundred times over. He really is the master of the legal thriller and The Judge's List is just more evidence of that. His books always draw me in from the first few pages and leave me needing to read more. I binged this book in one lazy Saturday at home during lockdown and I am not sorry about it. I will read anything this man writes and have been doing so for many many years now. The Judge's List sees us reunited with Lacey Stolz from The Whistler. It is 3 years later and she is almost 40 and trying to work out what she wants from life. Her job at the Florida Board on Judicial Conduct is not exciting her anymore and she is contemplating a change. That is until a mysterious phone call leads to case like no other she has ever worked on. The FBJC does not do murder cases, but there has never been an allegation that a sitting judge was a serial killer before. We know from early on who the killer is, a very clever and cunning judge who has a list of people who have wronged him in his life. He is patient and doesn't leave any evidence behind. But somebody has figured him out now. It is a page turner, and you will not see the ending coming. I certainly didn't. It was a WHAT moment at midnight that made me applaud the brain of John Grisham. Never a dull moment as we watch Lacey and her team try to get the evidence to take the judge down. Thank you to Hachette Australia for sending me an advanced copy of this book to read. Out on October 19th.

More Lacy Stoltz. More Lacy Stoltz. More Lacy Stoltz. This second book in the Whistler series gives Lacy a tricky dilemma to untangle. A woman wants to remain anonymous while reporting a sitting judge guilty of multiple murders. A serial killer is on the loose and this sociopath has on-line skills that keep him ahead of law enforcement while highly capable of tracking down his victims. Who will be next? Jeri Crosby, the woman who has been tracking him since her father's death twenty years ago? Lacy Stoltz, the interim director for the Board on Judicial Conduct? This rises to the top of the pack for me in the field of Grisham's novels. I enjoy a woman protagonist and in this one we get two. There is plenty of cloak and dagger as well as a thrilling game of cat and mouse in multiple contexts. Finally, this is a legal thriller without any political strings attached. It is just downright entertaining. Mr. Grisham, please give us another Lacy Stoltz book soon. With the future she has planned, there would be many ways for her to stumble upon another legal dilemma to untangle. A big thank you to Doubleday and NetGalley for a DRC in exchange for an honest review.

This book is filled with all the things that I love from Grisham… A tight story, a page turning legal thriller, a desire to see justice prevail… Especially...When, well, I can’t say... Because...Then I would be spoiling it – But...Then again, maybe the title does in a way. No, don’t try and guess it – just read it! By the way, you need not have read The Whistler to read this one. It can be a stand-alone.

I have read a few books by this author (The Firm, The Partner, The Broker, and The King of Torts) but that was way before I have a blog so I don’t have links to my reviews. I believe I loved them all including this one. I was hooked to this story. I haven’t read a book where a judge was accused of murder before. The characters were well developed and well liked. The main character somewhat worried about herself being unmarried with no kids approaching 40 but at the same time enjoyed her freedom and her own space. I have a friend in that situation and I know the struggle. The other character, Margie lead an exciting and lonely life of collecting information from her father’s killer. I liked that the killer’s view appeared as Lacy investigated Kronke, a victim. It explained how the event happened without speculation. This book followed Lacy, 39 years old lawyer as she received an anonymous phone call from a woman who referred to herself as Margie, 46. She wanted a private meeting with Lacy to ask for her professional opinions. Lacy, for 12 years, has been specializing in investigating judges who are accused of wrongdoing. Margie said an active judge killed her dad among many others and hoping if Lacy will take on her complaint. Lacy was bored with her current job and thought that this new accusation sounded intriguing. Accusing a judge of murder is rare. Lacy decided to hear her out. Lacy has an older brother Gunther and an FBI boyfriend named Allie. There’s a surprise view of the killer. There were many views after that including Margie, which was not her real name because she feared for her safety. She had been stalking her father’s killer for 20 years and knew that the killer had been killing up to 8 victims. She hoped that Lacy can send the killer to jail. The Judge’s List was well written and a fast paced read. A little too many point of views than I care for but I do liked the detailed view of the killer and the persons chasing the killer. I liked that the killer was created as a smart person, one who stayed a couple of steps ahead of the police. It was thrilling to read when the stalking was reversed, the killer knew he was being stalked. Definitely interesting also to see how technology was utilized for good and for bad. The ending was good and I didn’t guess the course of action. This book has good diversity. Although it’s a book 2 in a series, it can be read as a standalone. I haven’t read a legal thriller in awhile but sure won’t be my last. I recommend everyone to read this book! xoxo, Jasmine at www.howusefulitis.com for more details Many thanks to Doubleday Books for the opportunity to read and review. Please be assured that my opinions are honest.

A gripping continuation of John Grisham's The Whistler series.The Judge’s List by John Grisham is a chilling legal thriller that follows an investigation into a sitting judge who may be a serial killer. With a tense, slow-burn pace and sharp twists, it’s a dark and compelling read that keeps you guessing until the end. I loved the very unique and unsettling premise, a judge, sworn to uphold the law is suspected of being a calculating serial killer. The tension builds as investigator Lacy Stoltz gets closer to the truth, knowing her target is smart, powerful, and always one step ahead. This chilling cat-and-mouse dynamic keeps the suspense high and the reader hooked.

This one, IMHO, is the author at his best. Loved it, hated to put it down and was upset that keeping my husband fed and the need for sleep got in the way of polishing it off in one sitting. It's actually the second in a series featuring attorney Lacy Stoltz, but it stands alone quite well. I say that because although I read the first book, The Whistler, it was so long ago (2016) that I don't remember a thing except that I thoroughly enjoyed it as well. Here, Lacy is working for the Florida Board on Judicial Conduct, which investigates allegations against members of the judiciary, and has an FBI boyfriend named Allie Pacheco. Their relationship is serious, but so far it hasn't progressed to a ring-on-the-finger stage. One day, Lacy gets a call from a woman who calls herself Margie; she wants Lacy's agency to look into a judge she insists murdered her father years ago, when the judge wasn't even on the bench. But wait, there's more; Margie - real name Jeri Crosby - claims to have some evidence that her father isn't the judge's only victim (far from it, in fact). Even though Jeri says several other victims had unsatisfactory interactions with the judge, thereby providing him with motive, Lacy is skeptical (lawyers, after all, rely on actual evidence, which is noticeably missing in all these instances). Lacy also makes it clear that if evidence is found, her agency will have to turn the case over to the police and/or FBI - and Jeri's identity, which she's intent on keeping private for fear of her life - most likely would be revealed. As the story progresses, readers also get a glimpse into what the judge himself is up to, and one thing is clear: He's guilty as all get-out. Unfortunately, he's also smart, manipulative and has no intention of stopping until he makes his way through the list of people he believes have wronged him over the years. As circumstances in Lacy's agency open up new possibilities, she agrees to at least look into the case with help from her task force members Darren and Sadelle. Once they start delving into past murders (all with at least one common M.O.) and the victims' connections to the judge, it becomes clear they're dealing with a serial killer. Now, they must collect enough evidence to file a formal complaint on behalf of Jeri (under a fictitious name). But that also will mean the judge knows they're on to him, raising the question of how far he will go to avoid charges and protect his good name. In fact, it's a pretty sure bet it will be far enough that lives that aren't on the judge's original list find themselves on it now.

Never one to shy away from reality, Michael Connelly’s new novel, The Dark Hours brings it home. It’s in The Dark Hours that Detective Renee Ballard does her best work. She is a night owl and she loves flying solo. When a homicide occurs on her watch in the Late Shift, she wants it, even if the investigation should go to the detectives in the Hollywood Division. Once she dives into the case, what she finds, makes her want it even more. Her case links to an old unsolved crime, a cold case of retired Detective Harry Bosch’s, and wouldn’t you know it, the two decide to work together to solve them both. Ballard, of course, investigates other crimes as well, one of which involves several women assaulted in their homes, in the middle of the night, by a group called The Midnight Men, which brings about a different type of danger altogether. THE DARK HOURS is Michael Connelly’s best novel in years. It is an excellent police procedural but more than just a police procedural. Connelly looks at the current policing situation, and the local environment, with clear journalistic eyes, turning the background for the criminal investigations into an explicit observation of Los Angeles today. The primary story contains two cases — a pair of serial rapists working together (called the “midnight men”) and a murder that was meant to look like an accident. Renee Ballard is working the serial rapist case on New Years Eve when she is asked to call what appears to be the “accidental” death of a man that she almost immediately recognizes as a murder. It is the murder that takes her to Harry Bosch, because the bullet casing ties it to one of his old unsolved cases. This is definitely a Renee Ballard novel. Bosch helps her tie the pieces together on the murder case and provides backup support when she gets a lead on the midnight men case, but Ballard is the book’s main protagonist. As always, Connelly provides excellent descriptions of the routine details involved in running a police investigation. But it is the background that makes this more than just another police procedural. Sixty years ago, I lived in the Los Angeles area where these cases unfold, and so I can strongly visualize the changes to the environment that Connelly so vividly describes, changes fuelled by the opioid crisis and magnified by the pandemic. This is the first book I’ve read that so accurately depicts these horrors. The novel is near perfect. The only criticism I have is that Ballard seems, to me, to think too much like a male. Yes, she’s tough, but lots of tough women now appear in crime books, and they have never left me with the niggling doubt that the author doesn’t have an accurate grasp on how females think. It may be just me — I had a hard time putting a finger on any one aspect of Ballard’s behaviour that made me question her psychological gender. Maybe it is how she covers up for her coworker who is a slacker. Females treat female coworkers differently than men treat male coworkers.

As an avid reader, it's been interesting to me that authors of many of the books I've read over the past couple of years that are set in the present somehow manage to totally avoid what's going on in the world - most notably, the COVID-19 pandemic. A couple have set the time frame slightly before or slightly after, while others simply avoid the issue and carry on with their stories as if it didn't exist. Now comes a story that hits it - and other political goings-on - square on the nose (or more accurately, on the mask that's covering the nose). If I appreciated nothing else in this book, I'll give kudos for that. That said, it gets my vote for many other reasons, including an intriguing and attention-holding plot and competent, well-developed characters. That I've come to love them over previous books helps, of course, but overall that doesn't matter much; even if there's an occasional clinker amid the series (to which no author is immune), the characters are strong enough to carry the plot and result in a positive rating. For sure, though, this one's no clinker. Detective Renee Ballard is assigned to the West Hollywood Police Department's Sexual Assault team; checking out a homeless area under an overpass is where this story begins - as do the references to the vagaries of vaccinations and masking (Renee actually contracted the virus, which knocked her out of action for three weeks; now, she's been vaccinated and is very careful about wearing a mask herself). Most recently, she's been on the trail of a "tag team" of rapists who have struck twice. Here, a man is shot - perhaps accidentally - and it turns out the bullet came from the gun that was used in one of retired Detective Harry Bosch's cases back in 2011 (interestingly, while Harry has some health issues, he says he's not been vaccinated "yet," so Renee wears a mask when they interact in person). Although Harry's murder book seems to have inexplicably disappeared from the department, he saved enough information for them to hit the ground running with their investigation. And then, Renee gets a call saying that the "Midnight Men" rapists have struck again. Now she's got two cases to worry about, but as the murder investigation with Harry heats up, she gets the order to turn it over to a different unit. Never one to follow the letter of the law (on occasion, she's been known to stomp on it), Renee refuses to let go, although she and Harry try to stay under the radar while they try to find a link between his 2011 case and the current shooting. Much more than that I can't say without revealing too much, except that it's a thoroughly engrossing adventure that I didn't want to put down until I had to - and even then, I polished it off in two days of spare time. In short, another one well done and highly recommended!

The latest Michael Connelly thriller is set in the winter of 2021 in a U.S. ravaged by the pandemic and where the political divides are extreme and frequently violent. Situations which leave most members of the Los Angeles Police Department completely demoralised. Whilst hunting for a pair of serial rapists, nicknamed the Midnight Men, Detective Renee Ballard is called to the killing of Javier Raffa, a former gang member, on New Year’s Eve. She soon determines it is murder and ballistics reveal the same weapon was used in an earlier unsolved killing, that of record producer Albert Lee. Coincidentally, the detective who worked that case is the now-retired Harry Bosch. Despite their age/gender/ethnic differences, Renee and Harry are very much cut from the same cloth: the sort of detectives who always work for the victim and pursue their cases to the bitter end; often to the detriment of their careers. The novel proceeds with Renee working both cases with little help, and often hindrance, coming from her fellow officers, including her immediate superior. The only one she can always rely on in Harry. This is a superlative procedural thriller. Brilliantly paced and plotted and capturing the mood of the turbulent times perfectly. Proving that, even after 30 years on the job, Michael Connelly is still at the top of his game.

Douglas Preston and Lincoln Child return to their original beginnings in the latest novel. Pendergast and Coldmoon are investigating a case which turns into a supernatural event as befitting Savannah. When this team of writers began, they had action adventures and supernatural events but through the years had steered away. Bloodless brings back the circle and I look forward to what will be next.

It isn’t often that authors can have a character so decidedly return to the roots of what made a book so intriguing in the beginning, but the writing team of Preston and Child have successfully done just this thing. FBI Agent Aloysius Pendergast began his fictional career by hunting a gigantic monster through the NY Museum of Natural History. Now, he’s chasing another, even larger monster through the streets and cemeteries of Savannah, Georgia. Pendergast has made a career of handling curious cases that often border on paranormal intrigue. So it is not surprising that though they are still recovering from the ordeal that became their last investigation, Pendergast, along with his recent partner Agent Armstrong Coldmoon, and his ward, Constance Greene, are intercepted by Assistant Director Pickett before they can part ways. A series of troubling murders has beset Savannah, and rumors of the bodies being found completely drained of blood seems tailor-made to Pendergast’s expertise. Will the investigators find proof that the legendary Savannah Vampire actually exists? A group of ghost hunters making a movie certainly hope so, even if part of the crew has to fake the evidence. Meanwhile, an overbearing Senator seeking re-election causes another complication to an already difficult investigation that includes twists with a device that can see into the future and the true identity/fate of D.B. Cooper from the famed unsolved mystery fifty years earlier. The authors, as usual, have done a superb job with well-developed plots, enormously well-researched locations and scenarios, and enough twists and turns for a roller coaster. For long fans of the series, I don’t want to give anything away about the relationship developments between certain characters. For those who have never read this series before, don’t be afraid to give it a shot. You will be able to pick up most of the important points, though I suggest after reading this book you go back and start the series from the beginning to see what you may have missed. I award this novel five stars and recommend Bloodless to fans of detective procedurals, thrillers, and paranormal stories. It really has something for everyone. Happy Reading!
