But also, I loved it because they are the embodiment of true love. The definition of soulmates. Their love is truly why I read romance, so thank you Abby Jimenez for giving us the chance to watch Samantha and Xavier fall in love and prove that "if he wanted to, he would." The side plot about Samantha’s mom having early onset dementia was devastating. I’m honestly tearing up just writing this. I’ve never personally experienced this with someone close to me, but my mom has, and so has one of my closest friends, and just hearing what it’s like for them, especially being a caretaker, gave me a glimpse into how mentally, physically, and emotionally exhausting it really is. Abby Jimenez did such an incredible job capturing that. It felt so real, and it added so much depth to the story. Watching Samantha move back home to help take care of her mom hit especially hard. It wasn’t just about caretaking. It was about returning to a full house, falling back into old family dynamics, and trying to navigate all of that while also losing pieces of her mom. Her whole family struggled to figure out a routine that worked for everyone, trying to live their own lives while still showing up for her mom in the way she wanted and deserved. And that’s what made it so heartbreaking. It showed how hard it is to find balance, especially when everyone’s stretched so thin. Caregivers often end up putting their own mental, emotional, and physical health last because they’re so focused on the person they’re caring for. It’s draining. And seeing that play out on the page just gutted me. But it also made me realize even more how much those in my own life dealing with this similar situation have struggled. I felt terrible for Samantha during all of this, but also for Xavier. Long-distance relationships are hard enough, but adding the weight of caretaking on one side? Absolutely heartbreaking. The distance didn’t lessen their love, but it definitely made the situation feel more desperate and isolating for both of them. 😭 I truly appreciated how Abby Jimenez wove the romance and caregiver storylines together. It all felt so raw and real. Like two threads of the same story instead of separate plot lines. It really shows what you’re willing to sacrifice for the people you truly love. Samantha would move across the country, put her own life and relationship on hold, and pour everything into caring for her mom. And Xavier would work himself to the bone just to afford time with Samantha, and give up any free moment just to hear her voice. He knew she couldn’t. So instead, he found ways to show up for her, even when it meant sacrificing something himself. It made the whole love story feel authentic and true. Three times by chapter three (which was insane) and one more time in chapter twelve, but never again afterwards. It almost seemed like it was something Abby Jimenez may have added in during a draft just as a placeholder but then the editors forgot to remove it. It was so random and gave me the ick. This book was excellent—and terrifying. There’s a reason I don’t read geopolitical thrillers: they would stress me out too much to be enjoyable. (I do read books of non-fiction; they just tend to not be about current events. I read the news, and that’s enough.) The plot that is pivotal to The Black Wolf is certainly plausible—just as the one that formed the basis of Louise Penny’s previous book, The Grey Wolf was—and, again, terrifying. Several of the more recent books in this wonderful series have made me squirm because of their focus on the world in which we’re living. I do miss the stories in the series that spent a lot of time in the idyllic (well, mostly) village of Three Pines and frequently involved murders whose causes lay deep in layers of the past. (Apparently I’m not the only one who feels this way; Louise Penny addresses this in her acknowledgments—not wanting to tell the same story “over and over”—so I get it. I simply miss spending most of her stories in Three Pines, where I really could live—a bistro, a bookshop, a bakery…what’s not to love?) Back to The Black Wolf. I don’t want to fill this snapshot with spoilers or any specific details about the plot; the book jacket handles that just fine. I’ll just say that I held my breath—a lot—and was not about to go to bed until I’d finished the book, just a few days after starting it. But as terrifying as the storyline is, it cannot begin to be as frightening as the absolute reality of the other issues that the book deals with—the influence of social media as a news source, the ability to manipulate and edit reality to produce false “truths” that too many people readily believe, and the rise and spread of conspiracy theories. There’s a reason that Animal Farm (which Reine-Marie had (surprisingly) never read and keeps calling “Animal House”) and 1984 are mentioned repeatedly. Fortunately, there are glimmers of humor, like one of my favorite characters confusing two very different things—sometimes at especially tense moments—throughout the book. But the book made me tense; I can’t stress that enough. But the last few pages contained moments that made me weepy—and not because they were sad. On the contrary. The moments that brought tears were reminders to focus on the gifts that the natural world offers. And that is the ultimate message—at least for me. Horrible things may be happening in the world and, even as aware we are of many of them, there is so much we don’t know. Yet, against the horror, there is beauty and it is a gift—and that is what we have to remember.

I took a brief break from my BookTube Prize reading when The Black Wolf became available at my local library. I don’t read mysteries often, but I’ve now read every installment by Louise Penny, and this latest entry shows exactly why I keep coming back. Penny’s writing remains funny, poignant, suspenseful, and remarkably humane. We’re pulled once again into the lives of the villagers of Three Pines, while the story simultaneously widens to include national and global concerns. This time, the plot—centered on a shadowy figure spreading lies, fueling division, and quietly building support across institutions—feels especially unsettling in its relevance. The idea of a hidden network manipulating fear and polarization gives the novel a prescience that’s hard to ignore. As always, the strength of the book lies not just in the mystery itself, but in the evolving relationships among recurring characters and the moral questions that underpin the narrative. Penny continues to balance intimate community storytelling with larger political and social themes in a way that few writers in the genre manage. One caution to new readers: this series really does need to be read in order. Each installment builds on the history and emotional depth established in previous books. It actually took me two novels before I was fully hooked—but once I was, I stayed. And with The Black Wolf, that long-term investment continues to pay off.

Great book! A page turned that keeps you guessing up until the end!

One could be forgiven for momentarily thinking that a book titled THE SUMMER HOUSE involves bodies passionately bouncing off of each other over the course of a week or two in June. James Patterson and Brendan DuBois’ novel is anything but that. Yes, there are bodies bouncing throughout the book, but not in the carnal sense. What we have here is a thriller from beginning to end, wrapped around the nugget of an intriguing and puzzling mystery. The Summer House was originally conceived, constructed and utilized as a seasonal retreat in rural Georgia for a wealthy family. However, over the decades, it passed outside of the family and gradually devolved into a by-the-month rental property, which, in the novel’s present, has fallen into disrepair and disrepute. Indeed, as the book opens, it is little more than a local hub for some small-time drug trade. Within the first few pages, it also becomes the scene of a horrific mass murder. The whodunit element of the story seems resolved almost immediately. Eyewitnesses, forensics and security footage from nearby businesses all demonstrate conclusively that an elite team of Army Rangers known as the Night Ninjas are the doers. Recently returned from Afghanistan, they are noteworthy and notorious for quickly and quietly attacking home bases and leaving carnage in their wake, which is exactly what occurred at the Summer House. The Army sends Major Jeremiah Cook and his team to investigate and make sure that all the t’s are crossed. Cook is an Army veteran and former NYPD detective. He bears scars and secondary limitations from combat action, but steadfastly refuses to let either prevent him from getting the job done. His squad, each of whom possesses a certain investigative skill set, accompanies him to look at what appears to be an open-and-shut case. Interestingly enough, no one, from the local sheriff to officers on the nearby military base, seems to want Cook and his men around. The Night Ninjas are not particularly well-liked, and the evidence seems incontrovertible. But Cook is determined to work the case by the numbers, even when the head of the Night Ninjas strikes a deal to plead guilty on the condition that the remaining members of his team are exonerated and released. Yet Cook can’t let things go, and when parts of the evidence begin to unravel, he follows a slender thread of truth back to a place where he had vowed never to return. His team, meanwhile, is experiencing life-threatening danger from an unexpected source. Truth and lives are at stake, and there is a significant question as to whether either or both will survive to the end of the book. Patterson and DuBois have collaborated on a number of occasions, but this is arguably the best of the works that their partnership has produced thus far, which is saying something. DuBois has been prolific on his own, and the considerable writing chops he brings to the table will keep you reading well into the night. Full of twists, turns and action, THE SUMMER HOUSE makes for terrific reading this summer and beyond. Reviewed by Joe Hartlaub

Stephanie Plum has been my constant companion for decades, but she never seems to get any older. We should all be so lucky! My thanks go to Net Galley and Atria Books for the invitation to read and review. This book is for sale now. Stephanie is a bounty hunter, working for her cousin Vinnie’s bail bond service. She tracks down no-shows, takes them to have their hearings rescheduled, and collects a commission. Her mother wishes fervently that she would get a normal job such as a bank teller, or just go ahead and marry long-time boyfriend Officer Joe Morelli, and keep house and raise kiddies. But Stephanie is long on independence, and she’s short on marketable skills, and so this is what she does. And we readers are well aware that she wouldn’t be half this hilarious as a housewife, so we cheer her on. In an interview, author Evanovich said she had lit on the idea of a bounty hunter protagonist because the writer doesn’t need a background in legal matters the way that she would if she used a cop, detective, or lawyer. The primary skill required of a bail bonds enforcer is lying, and she felt she had a good grasp of that one. You gotta love it. There have been a few wobbles in the series, and a moment (long ago) when I thought perhaps it was played out. But like her intrepid protagonist, the author rallied and came back stronger than ever. Can you read this book if you haven’t read any of the others in the series? Yes. Yes, you surely can; but you are most likely going to want to go back for the rest once you do so. There are a few things that strike me as I read this one. I suddenly find myself wondering why Stephanie doesn’t seem to have women friends. She’s lived in Trenton—in the Burg—her entire life, so shouldn’t she have a few lifelong pals? But by the end of the story, I realized that her work buds are her go-to girls. Lula gets into a scrape and leaves what little she has to Stephanie (but of course, Lula pulls through. I don’t feel like this is a spoiler; since when would a riotously funny writer like Evanovich off a main character?) Connie is a distant relative, but she’s also a friend. I also find myself, like other reviewers, wondering about the sanitized language and decreasing vocabulary levels. We’ve been drifting in this direction for awhile. At the start of the series, profanity was used by the people and in the situations where you’d expect to find it. The overall language level was accessible to anybody that finished eighth grade. Over the last several episodes, however, it’s been drifting downward. Now, apart from one “damn”, I found nothing, although the euphemisms are stellar (“What the fork,” “What the Hellman’s Mayonnaise,” “Son of a bagel.”) And the overall vocabulary level is now down to about fifth grade. If it goes any lower (see the author’s other series,) I may not be interested anymore, but as it stands, it’s fast, it’s snappy, and I’m in. The usual elements—escorting Grandma Mazur to viewings at the mortuary; exploding cars; men surprising Stephanie when they let themselves into her locked apartment; dinner with Stephanie’s parents; a geeky witness, or victim, or possibly even an offender, that Stephanie takes under her wing; and the red-hot Joe Morelli are all present and accounted for. Stephanie’s mother has been drinking heavily every time Stephanie gets into a dangerous scrape, and Evanovich has been toying with some character development in her direction. I hope she follows through. The tension of Stephanie trying to decide between Morelli and the mysterious Ranger is over, for now, at least, and it was getting old, so I applaud this development. She knows that Ranger will never marry her, and there’s a lot he’ll never tell her. She knows Morelli. They grew up together, and they understand one another. Marriage, maybe not yet; but Joe is the one. She’s tempted by others in this installment, but for once, she behaves herself. Good. Whereas this series isn’t the magnificent literary accomplishment attained by some mystery Grand Masters, and it doesn’t try to be, I rate it as five stars in the humor genre. It made me laugh out loud on page two, and though I read quite a lot of books each year, those that have made me howl this year can be counted on one hand. It’s a more valuable characteristic than some might guess, especially during these tense times. Highly recommended to those that need a good laugh.

4.5 stars I am a LONG time Janet Evanovich reader…she and I have been together pretty much all of my adult years! 😳🥳 I recently read and thoroughly enjoyed her latest release, Game On: Tempting Twenty-Eight. It is a super fun, humorous, entertaining addition to the light-hearted quirky, comedic, numbered, mystery series. It has all the characters we have grown to love, even some from the past make an appearance. It’s also chock-full of the quintessential antics we’ve come to expect from the disastrously, delightful duo of Stephanie and Lula. Her stories are my tried and true. They are the perfect literary comfort food: familiar, easy-reading that I know will put a smile on my face. I always look forward to revisiting this series and can count on them for a good time. Please don’t stop writing ✍️
